newsitem.title: HONG KONG: New CEPA bid may be too late - analysts. [CORRECTED 14:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: New CEPA bid may be too late - analysts. [CORRECTED 14:55 GMT]

text.p: A counter bid by Malaysia's YTL Corp for Hong Kong's Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd (CEPA) may come too late, analysts said on Friday. (Corrects from "may have come too late" to "may come too late" to make clear new bid has not yet been made.)
"I think it's too late. Hopewell has already committed to the Southern deal. The only chance is that other shareholders of CEPA don't agree," said UBS Securities analyst Vincent Chan.

Just two weeks after CEPA parent Hopewell Holdings Ltd agreed to sell most of its stake in the unit to Southern Co's Southern Electric International, CEPA said on Friday it had been approached by YTL about the possible acquisition of a controlling stake.

"The board of directors of CEPA wishes to advise that...it has received an approach from YTL for possible acquisition of a controlling interest in CEPA. However, the board of directors of CEPA would like to emphasise that no offer or formal proposal has been received from YTL," it said in a statement.

Hopewell said on Friday that it had "irrevocably undertaken" to vote its shares in favour of the Southern deal. Southern aims to acquire 80 percent of CEPA through a straightforward cash deal of HK$18.50 per share, or a cash and stock offer.
Hopewell owns a 60.4 percent stake in CEPA. The Southern deal requires the approval of 75 percent of CEPA shareholders, of Hopewell shareholders and of its bankers.
Officials at YTL in Malaysia were not immediately available for comment. A spokesman for Hopewell and CEPA referred calls to financial advisor Peregrine Capital.
Officials there were not available for comment.
Southern Electric also remained tight-lipped.
"We are still maintaining a no comment position," regional director Ray Harris said.
Analysts said YTL would have to offer a substantially higher price for CEPA for its shareholders to beat Southern's bid.
"I would suspect it is going to have to be maybe 10 percent better or something," said Michael Breukels, utilities analyst at Nikko Research.
A successful bid would require YTL taking a "very aggressive stance", said Chan. He puts CEPA's net asset value at HK$14.00.
"If you pay in cash a higher price than HK$18.50... you need to have very aggressive valuation," he said.

Breukels said YTL may also have a hard time convincing minority CEPA shareholders, who would look towards the majority shareholder for direction, and the Malaysian infrastructure developer and power firm may also run into other difficulties.

"Given that YTL is coming in so late, if they are really trying to get an accurate assessment for themselves as to what the value of CEPA would be, they are going to have a pretty close look at CEPA books and their business dealings and what is coming on the pipe," he said.
"A company like Southern would have some serious objections as to future potential competitors having a look at CEPA at this stage," Breukels said.

Analysts said if YTL wanted to take control of CEPA, its offer would also need the approval of Hopewell management. Chan saw no interest in YTL launching a bid for the 40 percent of CEPA that Hopewell did not own.
"YTL can only buy 40 percent. You still cannot control the company and in order to control CEPA you have to get management support," he said.
-- Hong Kong newsroom (852) 2843 6345
